doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Calliope on Roller Coaster and the studio-jazz double life
summary: He played calliope on a Schifrin score, imitated styles on request, and played jazz seven to ten nights a month alongside studio work.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: I did. On a movie that Lalo Schiffrin wrote the score on. It was called “Roller Coaster.” And interestingly the whole score was just for keyboard instruments. I think there were six or seven of us. And pipe organ was on that score too. It was a terrible movie but a great score. But at the same time I was doing studio work I was playing jazz. The only thing I couldn’t really do was go on the road for extended periods of time because as a studio player – then and now – if you get a call with a contractor you want to take it so that you get the next one and the next one. And if you’re out touring a lot, you know you can’t. But you know I would have died emotionally and spiritually if I had only done studio work. I had to be doing – not that it wasn’t creative at times. You know we didn’t just play the written note but we were often called upon to improvise, to sound like (get me the “Shearing sound”; get me some Floyd Cramer; can you cop some Jerry Lee Lewis on this?). You know. So it was challenging and fulfilling to do that work but I also – I was probably playing jazz, I don't know, seven to ten nights a month while I was doing the studio thing. Because there was a lot of work in L.A. for jazz at that time. There were a lot of clubs and places to do concerts. So I had a double life going and enjoyed it very much.
